title: Read and respond to a range of text types

lessons.title: Different kinds of text
lessons.html:
Texts are all around us

A text is anything with words or pictures that gives a message. At work and at home you read many kinds of text every day.

Texts on the farm

  • Signs: No Smoking, Danger, Keep Out, Wash Hands.
  • Labels: on chemical containers, feed bags, medicine bottles.
  • Notices: on the notice board about meetings, pay day or a new rule.
  • Forms: leave forms, time sheets, store issue slips.
  • Instructions: how to start a pump, how to mix feed.
  • Letters and messages: a letter from the manager, an SMS or WhatsApp from your supervisor.
  • Pictures and symbols: a skull and crossbones means poison; a flame means it can burn.

Why the type of text matters

Each kind of text has a job. A sign tells you quickly what to do or not to do. A label gives you important facts about the product. A form asks you to give information. When you know what kind of text it is, you know how to read it.

Look before you read

Before you read, look at the text:

  1. Look at the heading or title. What is it about?
  2. Look at the pictures, colours and symbols.
  3. Look for words in big or bold letters. They are often the most important.
  4. Ask yourself: who wrote this, and what do they want me to do?

Red often means danger or stop. Yellow often means be careful. Green often means safe, or first aid.

Practice

Look at the notice board at work. Find one sign, one notice and one form.

lessons.title: Reading for meaning
lessons.html:
Understanding what you read

Finding the main idea

The main idea is the most important message of the text. Read the heading and the first sentence. Then ask: what is this text mostly about?

Example notice: Staff meeting on Friday at 07:00 at the workshop. We will talk about the new transport times. All workers must attend.

The main idea is: there is a meeting on Friday that everyone must go to. The details are the time (07:00), the place (workshop) and the topic (transport times).

Finding details

When you need one fact, you do not have to read every word. Look quickly for it. On a feed bag, look for the words for the animal, the mass of the bag and the date. On a time sheet, look for your name and the dates.

New words

When you find a word you do not know:

  • Read the sentence again. The other words may help you guess.
  • Look at the pictures.
  • Ask your supervisor or a co-worker.
  • Use a dictionary or a phone.

Is it fact or opinion?

A fact can be checked: The tank holds 5 000 litres. An opinion is what someone thinks: This is the best tank. Both can be in one text. Know which is which.

Reading safety labels

Chemical labels have very important words. Look for: the name of the product, the warning words (such as Danger or Caution), the pictures that show what protective clothing to wear, and first aid steps. If you cannot read or understand a label, do not use the product. Ask your supervisor.

lessons.title: Responding to texts
lessons.html:
Doing something with what you read

To respond means to act or answer after reading. Different texts need different responses.

Ways to respond

TextHow you respond
Safety signFollow it. Do not smoke where it says No Smoking.
NoticeGo to the meeting, tell your team
InstructionDo the steps in the right order
FormFill it in neatly and correctly
MessageReply, and say if you understand

Filling in a form

  1. Read the whole form first.
  2. Use a pen and write clearly, in block letters if asked.
  3. Fill in every part that applies to you: name, worker number, date.
  4. Check the dates and numbers.
  5. Sign where it says signature.
  6. Ask for help if you do not understand a question.

Talking about a text

Sometimes you respond by speaking. You may tell your co-workers what a notice says, or tell your supervisor that an instruction is not clear. Say what the text says in your own words. If you do not agree with something, say so politely and give your reason.

Asking questions

It is fine to ask. Good questions are: What does this word mean? When must this be done? Who must I give the form to?

Key points

  • Signs, labels, notices, forms and instructions are all texts with different jobs.
  • Look at the heading, pictures and big words before you read.
  • Find the main idea first, then the details you need.
  • Never use a chemical if you cannot read or understand its label.
  • Respond correctly: follow, fill in, reply or ask.
